description: Hardwear.io USA talks from Hardwear.io USA 2024.

talks.title: Exposing Critical Threats In Millions Of Connected Devices - Alexander; Sergey
talks.teaser: Researchers trace firmware flaws in a widely deployed cellular modem from local midlet abuse to full remote compromise over SMS.
talks.summary:
Cellular modems sit inside cars, medical gear, payment terminals, industrial systems, and laptops, yet public vulnerability data for one heavily used module was almost empty before this work. The presenters map the software stack—firmware, applications, remote control, and privileged Java midlets—and explain why midlet confidentiality features blocked normal filesystem listing while leaving integrity weak.

Firmware came from decapping NAND and rebuilding logical flash blocks; JTAG on the baseband processor was abandoned after probing. Analysis of installed midlets uncovered paths to leak hidden storage locations, abuse FTP-related AT commands, and overwrite permission files to reach manufacturer privilege locally without reverse engineering the whole native image. Deeper firmware review found hundreds of AT commands, vendor script namespaces, and fuzzing that surfaced a heap overflow on the command interface, plus a SUPL SMS fragmentation bug that overflows heap buffers and enables controlled crashes.

Using slow memory disclosure through fault logs, they built write primitives, unlocked vendor memory read/write namespaces, executed injected code, and activated OTA provisioning to install a persistent midlet—demonstrating end-to-end remote compromise from SMS alone. They reported two critical issues to the vendor, plan a fuller paper, and urge disabling non-essential SMS, enforcing midlet signature checks, and limiting physical AT access where feasible.

talks.title: TPM 2.0 Attestable Firmware: Recovering Trust After Firmware Flaws
talks.teaser: Shows how TPM-based attestation can restore trust after firmware bugs, using version-unique secrets and a smaller trusted base.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how a machine can prove which software it runs after a bug is found and patched, and where a TPM fits into that proof. Because bugs are unavoidable, fleets need a recovery plan that can be verified remotely. Measured boot records each mutable component before it runs, and the TPM keeps the secrets used to vouch for those measurements. A leak of those secrets would break attestation and recovery, which makes the TPM part of the trusted computing base.

The proposed fix shrinks that base to a small bootloader that measures the firmware and derives a unique secret for each version, so a leaked old version cannot reveal a newer secret. The speakers showed how a TPM create-primary command can mix that secret into new keys without touching existing seeds, and how an endorsement key can be certified through an embedded CA, following the DICE approach. In a Titan chip demo, a memory check bug was found and patched, then a rollback attempt failed its integrity check because the version secret had changed.

The takeaway is that code should be attestable so recovery can work at scale. The speakers urged TPM vendors to implement the optional feature in the newest library specification and customers to ask for it. In Q&A they said the design guards against leaked seeds as well as downgrades, and needs only persistent bootloader-readable data that later firmware can be locked out of.

talks.title: Panel: A New Root Of Trust: Changing Computing With TEE
talks.teaser: Explains how trusted execution environments use hardware attestation and memory encryption to keep data safe from cloud hosts.
talks.summary:
This panel introduces trusted execution environments (TEEs) as a new root of trust for cloud computing. The panelists contrast them with TPMs: a TPM attests the hardware and firmware, but applications run unencrypted, whereas a TEE encrypts the memory of a protected environment so that a host, hypervisor or administrator cannot read it. A hardware-signed attestation report lets a user check that the environment is genuine and in a known good state before sending sensitive data. The reference values come from endorsements across the hardware, firmware and software supply chains.

The discussion then turns to trust and verification. The speakers argued that users should be able to validate attestations themselves, not rely only on a third-party verifier, which matters for auditing if a verifier is later compromised. They listed current options from Intel, Arm, AMD and Nvidia GPUs, and used a confidential AI example in which a financial firm wants to run proprietary models in the cloud. Intel's TDX Connect was described as a direct link that lets devices reach a trust domain, while current device I/O relies on shared memory with extra copying. On performance, they said modern memory encryption costs below 1 percent, while communicating with other devices or the network still carries a penalty.

Toward the end, the panelists stressed the limits of TEEs: they do not stop physical attacks, denial of service or very low-level hardware probing, and scope depends on the implementation. Open source was debated, with the view that credibility, not just open code, builds trust. Intel pointed to its TDX module source code and bug bounty program as ways to invite review. The practical takeaway was that attestation has to be built into deployment, and that firmware supply chains are harder to inspect than software ones.

talks.title: SRAM Data Remanence In SoCs: Covert Storage And Exfiltration Risks In TEE
talks.teaser: Shows how SRAM aging can hide covert data in chips and leak TrustZone secrets through accelerated power-on state readout.
talks.summary:
The talk examines data remanence in SRAM, the on-chip memory used for microcontroller caches and scratchpads, whose power-on state can retain traces of earlier values. The speaker explains that a bit held in an SRAM cell slowly shifts the race between the two cross-coupled inverters, so the cell later powers up with a predictable value. Heating the chip and raising its voltage shortens this aging from years to a few hours. On that basis the speaker builds a plausibly deniable covert channel. Error correction and counter-mode AES make the hidden data recoverable, and encrypting it pushes the power-on statistics close to those of a clean device.

The second part turns to trusted execution environments such as Arm TrustZone. Secure and normal worlds share the same physical SRAM and cache lines, so an attacker with physical access can use accelerated aging to read back secure contents. Reported results include recovering secure SRAM content with sub-3% accuracy without pre-characterization, narrowing the search space to about 8,000 keys when a cache line is pre-characterized, dumping Cortex-A L1 cache contents through a coprocessor interface after boot, and extracting a full AES operation that runs entirely in cache, with over 93% of the data recovered.

The closing discussion covers limits. Aging is largely irreversible, temperature has a much smaller effect than voltage, and software-only overvolting is constrained by the processor. For defenders, built-in memory self-test controllers that clear SRAM before software runs were suggested as a practical countermeasure, and the speaker noted that SRAM physical unclonable functions can be cloned with high accuracy under this attack.

talks.title: Building A Silicon Analysis Toolkit
talks.teaser: Shows how a hobbyist makes fuming nitric acid and builds a controlled decapping and microscope imaging rig at home.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how to remove the package from an integrated circuit to expose the silicon die, so it can be imaged and checked for things like counterfeiting or an embedded ROM, using equipment a home lab can afford. The speaker starts with making fuming nitric acid by distilling commonly sold chemicals. Safety guidance covers the workspace layout, fume extraction, choosing gloves that suit each chemical, and face protection. For storage, the speaker describes a two-container arrangement with a neutralizing bicarbonate layer and pH test strips as a leak indicator.

Next, the talk moves from pouring acid over chips to controlled etching. An industrial jet decapper worked but was poorly suited to one or two chips, and Kapton tape with a cut-out let acid creep under the adhesive. Viton O-rings seated in small PVC cups, held in a machined brass fixture, gave clean circular and rectangular openings, and PVC held up better than the speaker expected. Chips can sometimes still run after decapping, and gold bond wires tolerate the process better than copper.

For imaging, the build uses a top-down metallurgical microscope with a motorized stage. A 3D-printed Delta stage was stiff enough only after the mount was replaced with aluminum, and custom kinematics firmware on a low-cost microcontroller was written to accept standard motion commands. Focus stacking over a grid reduced roughly 8,000 raw frames to 675 images, which were stitched in ImageJ in blocks. The takeaway is that a modest setup can produce a high-resolution die image for inspection.

talks.title: Panel: The Right To Secure; What, Who, How And Why!
talks.teaser: Panelists debate whether owners of end-of-life embedded and industrial devices should get a legal right to apply security fixes.
talks.summary:
This panel asks whether owners and operators should have a legal right to secure embedded devices that vendors no longer support. The discussion centers on end-of-life equipment in critical infrastructure where known vulnerabilities go unpatched because the manufacturer will not issue a fix and no one else is permitted to change the firmware. The panelists separated this from right to repair, which they described as mostly about cost and waste, and they discussed a 2023 manufacturer white paper that argued against repair rights on cybersecurity and intellectual property grounds.

One panelist, a reverse engineer, argued that researchers already patch devices without permission, so the real gap is whether owners can deploy those fixes legally. That work involved patching a handheld radio's firmware, where editing code was manageable but missing test cases, hardware documentation and hardware variants caused lasting problems. An operator said over 50 percent of the equipment still in use is effectively unsupported, that warranty and insurance terms often make modifications a liability, and that changing controllers is hard to validate at scale. Panelists also cited DARPA's micro-patching research as a sign that automated firmware changes are becoming practical.

Proposals for a path forward included treating reverse engineering of legally owned products as allowed under copyright law, asking insurers to assess embedded systems explicitly, and negotiating contract clauses that let owners apply fixes when vendors decline. The panel agreed that waiting for end of life is too late, but did not settle on a single legal request. Audience questions covered vendor lock-in and whether open source security history offers useful lessons for embedded devices.

talks.title: BarraCUDA: GPUs Do Leak DNN Weights
talks.teaser: See how side channel measurements can reveal neural network weights from a GPU, and why recovering them at scale remains costly.
talks.summary: Peter Horvath describes extracting neural network weights from a GPU using side channel measurements, focusing on an Nvidia Jetson with a Maxwell GPU. He explains the challenges of noisy measurements and uncertain warp scheduling, then compares leakage models and reports that recovering a weight took up to 20 million traces in their experiments. Attendees learn how the attack works, why scaling it to large networks is costly, and which countermeasures the researchers consider.

talks.title: Trimmed: Welcome Note John McMaster
talks.teaser: An opening welcome traces how a hands-on hardware security gathering grew from 2019 into a worldwide community with labs and tooling.
talks.summary:
The session opens the fourth United States edition in 2024 with a rallying call for hardware hacking rather than a technical deep dive. The presenter recalls struggling around 2014 to find Bay Area meetups focused on kernel work, reverse engineering, and opening real devices, which motivated interest in a dedicated hardware security community. He describes the first conference in 2019 as blending forward-looking research with practical workshops—USB reverse engineering, Bluetooth, hands-on gear, and demonstrations people could touch in person.

A keynote by Chris Tarnovski is highlighted as emblematic of the culture: satellite television card breaking, semiconductor challenges, and a contrast between underground hackers and formal industry dress at social events. The narrative follows how topics widened from narrow radio or USB niches toward large IoT, vehicles, and AI-scale systems, while events keep offering tools such as Pico EMP and hallway equipment like wire bonders and X-ray machines. Attendees from Brazil and France illustrate growing international draw.

The close emphasizes succession in the field—veterans alongside newer chip-focused researchers—and sponsor-backed lab gear as proof of momentum. The audience is urged to meet in the hallways and help raise expectations for what partners might bring next year.

talks.title: Secrets Of Simos18: REng The Secure Boot Mechanism Of An ECU
talks.teaser: Shows how a Volkswagen engine control unit's secure boot is bypassed through two exploit chains to run custom firmware.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the engine control unit in a 2016 Volkswagen Golf 7R, a TriCore microcontroller module whose firmware is protected by secure boot and signed updates. The speaker explains the setup used for the work: a Raspberry Pi acting as a CAN bus interface, the UDS reprogramming flow used by dealer tools, and the seed-and-key unlock. Early attempts to read memory, use calibration protocols, and find memory safety bugs in CAN handling turned up nothing usable. The immobilizer also meant the module had to stay installed in the car to be reprogrammed at all.

Static analysis of a partial firmware dump led to the customer bootloader, which held an AES key and IV in plain flash. With the decrypted image in hand, the speaker found that erasing one block and writing to another left the signature flag of the application block intact. That allowed code to be written over unerased flash, and a payload patched a sample-mode check so signature validation was skipped. A second chain targeted the supplier bootloader, reached through a timer-based pulse pattern on two pins. Its seed was an RSA challenge built from random bytes seeded by a 31-bit system timer, which could be enumerated. A CRC routine that could be pointed at protected flash, combined with reading RAM after a fast reset, exposed the stored flash unlock passwords.

The main takeaways are that signature checks are only as strong as the erase and write logic around them, that challenge randomness must not come from a predictable timer, and that secrets should not sit in plain flash. The speaker notes that newer ECUs use TrustZone, and the research tools were published on GitHub.

talks.title: State-of-the-Art Anti-Counterfeiting: Attacks And Countermeasures
talks.teaser: Explains how anti-counterfeiting chips are attacked and which countermeasures slow key extraction and cloning.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how authentication chips used in printer cartridges, batteries and medical consumables are built and attacked. The speaker argues that a valuable aftermarket makes these chips a target, and that a stolen production lot can be worth a large sum to a cloner. He describes staged key provisioning across design, wafer sort and final test, along with provenance tracking so that duplicate chip identities could be spotted.

Attacks are grouped by invasiveness, from passive probing to glitching, laser fault injection and invasive work. Power analysis can reveal keys from challenge-response operations, and differential fault attacks can extract them when a computation is corrupted. For non-volatile memory, the speaker shows how a test readback path or rewired bond pads could expose secret data, and suggests blocking readback, returning a CRC instead, and keeping secret data at a wider width than the user data path so a redirected read yields only a fragment.

Defenses discussed include mutual authentication, so the chip releases nothing until the verifier proves it knows the expected answer, and timing-based proof-of-work checks that act as a second factor. Physically unclonable functions are presented as weaker than often assumed, since their outputs and helper data can be copied, though they hold no secrets when powered down. The closing advice is to make reverse engineering slow and costly, forcing custom silicon, and to watch how chiplet designs complicate trust and supply chain control.
